title: Sell-through rate
reading_md:
**What it measures.** The share of the units received for a line that has sold, net of returns. Buyers use it during a season to spot lines that sell fast and lines that will need a markdown.

**Formula.**

Sell-through % = 100 × (units sold - units returned) / units received

- Units received: everything delivered for the line this season, so far.
- Units sold minus units returned: a sale that came back is not a sale.
- Grain: SKU (or line) × season to date.

**Worked example.** For the autumn season Voltmarkt received 1,200 units of a new 55-inch TV. By mid-November 900 had sold, and 60 of those came back.

- Sell-through = 100 × (900 - 60) / 1,200 = 70.0%.
- Leaving the returns in gives 100 × 900 / 1,200 = 75.0%, which overstates how much of the stock has really gone.
- If the returned TVs went back into stock, 360 are on hand now (1,200 - 900 + 60). Dividing sales by today's stock, 900 / 360, gives 250%, a meaningless number: stock on hand shrinks as the line sells.

**Reading the number.** Compare sell-through with the time gone in the season. 40% after 10 weeks of a 12-week season points to a markdown. 95% after 2 weeks may mean too few units were bought, so sales will be lost once the line runs out.

**Common mistakes.**

- Dividing by stock on hand instead of units received.
- Not subtracting returns.

**What sell-through does not answer.**

- Whether the line made money: that needs gross margin, after any markdown.
- How many weeks the remaining stock will last at the current pace: that is stock cover.
- Whether a line sold out because demand was strong or because too few units were bought.

**How managers ask for it.** "How is the autumn range selling through?" "Which lines will need markdown?"
